channel.description: Recent content in Api_available on Best of AI

item.title: AccuWeather
item.description:
AccuWeather provides weather forecasts for locations around the world. Its app and website show current conditions, hourly and 10-day forecasts, radar and satellite maps, and alerts for severe weather. A signature feature is MinuteCast, which predicts when rain or snow will start and stop at your exact location. Longer-range outlooks give a general sense of the weeks ahead, and features such as air quality and pollen cover health-related conditions.

For businesses, AccuWeather sells data and APIs that power weather information in other apps, media, retailers, utilities, and logistics. Meteorologists combine models, observations, and machine learning to produce its forecasts, and the company has developed AI tools for short-term forecasting and for delivering personalized alerts and impact information, such as how weather might affect travel or operations.

item.title: Azure AI Speech
item.description:
Azure AI Speech brings Microsoft’s speech technology into applications. Speech-to-text transcribes audio in real time or from recordings in many languages, with options for custom vocabulary and speaker separation. Text-to-speech offers a large library of neural voices in many languages and styles, with control over tone, speed, and emotion using SSML. Real-time speech translation converts spoken language into another language for captions or voice.

Additional features serve specialized needs. Custom Neural Voice lets approved customers build a branded voice from recorded samples, subject to a restricted-access process to prevent misuse. Voice live and conversational features support building voice agents, and avatar capabilities create talking presenters from text. Container deployments allow running models on premises or at the edge, and the service integrates with Azure OpenAI and other Azure AI tools.

item.title: Baidu ERNIE
item.description:
ERNIE, which stands for Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration, is Baidu’s answer to ChatGPT. The consumer chatbot answers questions, writes and edits text, generates images, and handles tasks in Chinese and other languages, and it is built into Baidu’s search engine and apps. It benefits from Baidu’s knowledge graph and search data, and is a major option for Chinese-language users.

For developers and companies, Baidu offers ERNIE models through its Qianfan cloud platform, with APIs, fine-tuning, and tools for building AI applications. The company has released versions of its models with open weights, which lets developers run them independently. The models support multimodal inputs and reasoning, and are used in enterprise products, cloud services, and Baidu’s autonomous driving and other businesses.

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: Bria
item.description:
Bria builds visual generative AI around licensing. Its models are trained on licensed data from content partners rather than scraped web images, and contributors share in revenue, which gives companies a clearer position on copyright than many alternatives. The company also offers indemnification to enterprise customers.

The product is delivered as APIs and tools for businesses. Capabilities include generating images from prompts, editing and background removal, creating product shots, and controls for brand consistency. Enterprises in advertising, e-commerce, and media can embed these features in their apps, with options for fine-tuning on their own assets.

item.title: Bruno
item.description:
Bruno is part of the group of tools for sending API requests, alongside Postman and Insomnia. Its approach is different: collections are saved in a plain text markup language as files in a folder, not in a vendor’s cloud. Teams commit them to git, review changes in pull requests, and keep API tests next to the code they test.

You can build requests with variables, scripts, and assertions, run collections for testing, and use it from a command line interface in CI pipelines. It supports REST, GraphQL, and other protocols. Because it works offline and does not require an account, it appeals to developers who dislike mandatory sign-ins and cloud syncing after changes in other tools.

item.title: Google Cloud Vision
item.description:
Google Cloud Vision is a set of pretrained image analysis features available through an API. Send an image, and it can return labels describing what it contains, detect objects and their locations, read printed and handwritten text, identify landmarks and logos, detect faces and emotions without identifying individuals, and flag explicit content with SafeSearch. It processes single images and batches, including scanned documents.

Typical uses include indexing photo libraries, extracting text from receipts and signs, moderating uploaded images, and powering search by image. Google offers related products for more specialized needs, such as Document AI for forms and Vertex AI for custom models and newer multimodal Gemini models that can describe and reason about images in more detail. Product search features help retailers match photos to catalogs.

item.title: NocoDB
item.description:
NocoDB turns a database into something that feels like Airtable. Connect it to an existing SQL database or create a new one, and users see tables as spreadsheets they can filter, sort, and edit, with views as kanban boards, galleries, calendars, and forms. Non-technical colleagues get access to data without learning SQL.

It generates REST and GraphQL APIs for tables, supports permissions and webhooks, and offers automation and an AI assistant to help with fields and queries. Because it is open source, teams can host it themselves and keep data on their own servers.

item.title: ReadMe
item.description:
ReadMe helps companies document their APIs. Teams upload an OpenAPI specification, and the platform generates an interactive reference with code samples in several languages and a try-it console that makes real requests with the reader’s own key. Guides and changelogs sit alongside, forming a single developer hub.

It is also a source of insight. API owners see which endpoints developers use, where requests fail, and which pages cause confusion, so documentation can improve based on evidence. Personalized docs show a logged-in developer their own API keys and data, which makes onboarding faster. An AI assistant answers questions from the documentation.

item.title: DhiWise
item.description:
DhiWise sits between design and development. A designer prepares screens in Figma, and DhiWise generates app code, including navigation, state management, and connections to APIs defined by a specification. The output follows common project structure, so developers can continue in their own tools.

It speaks to teams that build many similar screens and want consistency. Developers use it to produce the first version of the user interface and wiring, then refine business logic by hand. AI features add the ability to generate code from prompts and to adapt designs.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: OpenCode
item.description:
OpenCode is a coding agent that works in a developer’s terminal. It reads a repository, plans changes, edits files, and runs commands, with a text interface for conversation. The same engine also runs behind a desktop app, editor extension, and web client.

Provider freedom is the main appeal. Users connect models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, or open models run locally, and can switch between them. Configuration files add project rules, custom agents, and Model Context Protocol tools, and sessions can be shared.

item.title: Natural
item.description:
Natural addresses a gap in agent infrastructure: how an AI agent pays for things. Through its API, developers create an account for an agent, fund it, set spending rules, and let it pay vendors, receive money, or issue virtual cards for purchases.

Controls matter, since a spending agent can cause damage. Limits, approvals, and logs let the owner decide what an agent may buy and see what it did. The company positions this as payments infrastructure for a future where agents transact with each other and with businesses.

item.title: BrowserStack Test Companion
item.description:
Test Companion is an AI agent for quality assurance. Instead of a separate dashboard, it works in the developer’s editor, where it can generate test scripts from a description or from the code, run them on BrowserStack’s device and browser cloud, and investigate failures.

Maintenance is a major use. Tests break when interfaces change, and fixing them takes time. The agent can update selectors, adjust steps, and rerun, which reduces the upkeep that makes automated testing costly. It works with common frameworks and connects to BrowserStack’s testing infrastructure.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: FLUX
item.description: FLUX comes from Black Forest Labs, a company founded by researchers who previously worked on Stable Diffusion. Its models became popular because they produce sharp, detailed images that follow prompts closely, including difficult cases like readable text in a picture and complex scenes with several subjects. For many people, FLUX became the best open alternative to closed services such as Midjourney, because the weights for several versions can be downloaded and used locally.

item.title: Gemini Pro
item.description: Gemini Pro refers to the mid-sized models in Google’s Gemini family, positioned between the smaller, cheaper Flash models and the heaviest reasoning options. Google’s naming moves with each generation, but the idea stays the same: Pro is the version intended for demanding everyday work without the cost or delay of the very largest model. Gemini was designed from the start to take in several types of input at once, so the same model reads text, looks at images, listens to audio, and watches video rather than handing those jobs to separate systems.

item.title: GPT Image
item.description:
GPT Image brings image generation into the same model family that handles text. A user describes an image or uploads one to edit, and the model generates or modifies it, following detailed instructions and rendering readable text, which earlier image models struggled with. It can edit photos, change styles, and keep a subject consistent across images.

The model is available inside ChatGPT, where conversation lets users refine results step by step, and through the API for developers building apps. It replaced the DALL-E models in OpenAI’s lineup. Smaller and faster variants exist for cost-sensitive use.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: There's An AI For That
item.description:
There’s An AI For That, often shortened to TAAFT, started as a simple search for AI tools by task. A user types what they want to do, such as write a cover letter or remove a background, and gets a list of tools for that job, with ratings and descriptions.

Its size is the draw. It adds new tools constantly, offers an alert for launches, and includes pricing and user reviews. Some listings are promoted by makers.

item.title: Anyscale
item.description: Anyscale was founded by the creators of Ray, a framework that makes it easier to spread Python code across many machines. Ray is widely used in AI for tasks such as distributed model training, large-scale data processing, reinforcement learning, and serving models, and it is the engine behind a number of big AI systems. Anyscale offers a managed platform that handles cluster setup, scaling, and monitoring, so teams do not have to operate the infrastructure themselves.

item.title: Baseten
item.description:
Baseten runs models for companies that build AI products. A team packages a model, often with the Truss open-source tool, and deploys it as an endpoint that scales up and down with demand. The platform handles GPU provisioning, scaling, and monitoring, which are chores that distract from building the product.

It focuses on performance. Optimized inference engines, quick cold starts, and support for the latest GPUs help serve models with low latency and cost. Teams can deploy open models from a library, bring their own, or fine-tune, and use dedicated deployments for steady traffic. Options for running in a customer’s own cloud address security needs.

item.title: Cutout.Pro
item.description:
Cutout.Pro offers a set of web tools for common image tasks. Its background remover isolates a subject in a few seconds, and other features upscale resolution, colorize old photos, remove objects, retouch portraits, and generate passport-style photos. A bulk processing option helps stores prepare many product photos.

An API lets developers build these functions into their own products, and plugins connect with tools like Photoshop. Creators and sellers use it for listing photos, social content, and design assets, often at lower cost than hiring a retoucher.

item.title: DeepInfra
item.description:
DeepInfra hosts open models and sells access by the token or by usage. A developer picks a model from its catalog, which includes chat models, embeddings, image generators, and speech tools, and calls it with an API compatible with OpenAI’s format. The company handles GPUs, scaling, and optimization.

The appeal is price and simplicity. Because open models are widely available, hosting providers compete on cost and speed, and DeepInfra positions itself at the low end. Developers can also deploy custom models or fine-tuned versions in some cases, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Eden AI
item.description:
Eden AI addresses the problem of integrating many AI vendors. Each provider has its own API, formats, and billing. Eden AI offers one API for tasks like text generation, translation, OCR, speech recognition, image analysis, and more, and routes the request to the provider a developer chooses.

That makes comparison simple: the same input can be sent to several providers to see which gives the best result for the price. Fallback options switch to another provider if one fails, and a single bill and dashboard track usage. Workflows allow chaining several AI steps.

item.title: Firecrawl
item.description:
Firecrawl solves a common step in AI projects: getting web content into a form language models can use. A developer gives it a URL, and it fetches the page, handles JavaScript rendering, removes boilerplate, and returns clean Markdown. It can also crawl a whole site, map its links, or extract structured fields from pages using a schema.

Search and agent features expand its use. Developers can search the web and scrape results in one call, or use an endpoint that gathers data across many pages from a plain description. Integrations connect to frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex and to tools via the Model Context Protocol. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Lusha
item.description:
Lusha helps sales and recruiting teams get in touch with prospects. While viewing a profile on LinkedIn or a company website, a user clicks the Lusha extension to reveal contact information, then saves it to a CRM. A database search finds contacts by role, company size, and industry.

Additional features include intent signals, technology data, and enrichment of existing lists, as well as integrations with Salesforce, HubSpot, and sales engagement tools. The company emphasizes compliance with privacy laws and offers ways for people to opt out.

item.title: Minimax
item.description:
MiniMax builds models across modalities. Its Hailuo video generator produces short clips from text or images and became popular with creators for motion quality. The company also offers language models, speech synthesis, and music generation, available through apps and an API.

Developers use the API to add generation to products, and the consumer apps let users try the models directly. MiniMax has also released open-weight language models that have been used in agents and coding, adding to its profile among Chinese AI labs.

item.title: Neets AI
item.description:
Neets AI offers speech synthesis through a simple API. Developers send text and choose a voice, and the service returns audio. It emphasizes variety of voices, speed, and low cost, which suits projects that generate large volumes of audio, such as reading articles aloud.

Typical users include app developers, content publishers, and teams building voice agents. Voice quality is good for many purposes, though the top-tier commercial providers may offer more emotion and control. Streaming support makes it usable for interactive applications.

item.title: Patch
item.description:
Patch simplifies buying carbon removal. Companies browse projects, compare prices and methods, and purchase credits through a platform or API instead of negotiating deals one by one. Developers can embed purchases into other software, such as financial or e-commerce products.

The company has shifted toward helping enterprises plan and procure carbon removal at scale, with tools for sourcing, due diligence, and reporting. AI supports tasks like drafting requests for proposals and evaluating projects.

item.title: SambaNova
item.description:
SambaNova designs custom chips, called reconfigurable dataflow units, along with the software and systems around them. The goal is high-speed inference and training for large language models at lower power than general-purpose GPU setups.

Its cloud service offers fast access to open models through an API, and enterprises can deploy systems on premises for data control. Government and large organizations are among its customers.

SambaNova is sold on usage-based cloud pricing and system contracts. The company has faced a competitive field of chip makers and has been the subject of reports about funding and acquisition talks, so check its status. Alternatives include Groq, Cerebras, NVIDIA, Together AI, and Fireworks AI. SambaNova suits organizations needing fast inference.

item.title: Seamless AI
item.description:
Seamless.AI helps salespeople find who to contact. Users search by title, industry, and location, or use a browser extension to look up contacts on websites, and the platform returns emails and phone numbers pulled from public sources and its database. Lists export to CRMs and engagement tools.

Real-time search and enrichment aim to keep data fresh, and intent signals show which accounts may be in a buying cycle. AI features help write outreach and prioritize accounts.

item.title: Arcadia
item.description:
Arcadia has two sides. For consumers, it helps people use renewable energy even if they cannot install solar panels. Customers subscribe to a share of a local community solar project and receive credits on their utility bill, or choose plans that match their usage with renewable generation. The platform tracks bills and savings in one account.

For businesses, Arcadia offers access to utility data. It connects to thousands of utilities to pull bill and usage information through APIs, which energy software companies, solar developers, and sustainability teams use to analyze consumption. This data layer is a major part of its business and helps other companies build energy products.

item.title: Archbee
item.description:
Archbee helps teams write and publish documentation. The editor supports rich text, code blocks, diagrams, and embedded content, and spaces organize material into sections with navigation and search. Teams can keep docs private for internal use or publish them as polished public sites with custom domains and branding, which makes it suitable for product help centers and developer portals.

Features for technical documentation include API reference generation from OpenAPI specs, Git integration to sync docs with repositories, version control, and review workflows. AI features provide smarter search and an assistant that answers questions from your documentation, plus writing help. Analytics show which pages are read and what readers search for but cannot find.

item.title: AWS Rekognition
item.description: Rekognition lets developers add image and video analysis to an application without training a model from scratch. You send an image or a video and get back detected objects and scenes, text found in the picture, faces with attributes such as glasses or smiling, and flags for unsafe or inappropriate content. It works on photos, stored video files, and live video streams, and it integrates with S3, Lambda, and other AWS services.

item.title: Fauna
item.description:
Fauna set out to give developers a database that scaled globally without managing servers. It combined a flexible document model with relational features, offered strong consistency across regions, and was accessed through an API with its own query language, FQL, and earlier through GraphQL. Developers built web and mobile apps on it without running infrastructure.

The company announced that it would wind down its hosted service, and the service closed, with accounts deleted afterward. It also said it would release parts of its technology as open source, so some of the ideas may live on in community projects.

item.title: Geotab
item.description:
Geotab makes the small devices that plug into vehicles and report what they do. A device in the diagnostic port records location, speed, harsh braking, idling, engine fault codes, and more, and sends the data to the cloud, where fleet managers view it on maps and dashboards. Companies with delivery vans, service trucks, buses, and long-haul trucks use it to track vehicles, optimize routes, and reduce costs.

Analytics turn the data into insights. Driver scoring identifies risky behavior and supports coaching, maintenance alerts flag vehicles that need service based on engine data, and fuel and emissions reports support efficiency and electric vehicle planning. AI features include an assistant that answers questions about fleet data in natural language, and models that predict problems and rank safety risks. A marketplace of third-party apps extends the platform, and compliance tools support electronic logging rules.

item.title: GitBook
item.description:
GitBook helps teams publish documentation that people can actually navigate. Writers use a clean editor to create pages, organize them into spaces and collections, and publish them as a polished documentation site with search, navigation, and versioning. Software companies use it for product docs, API references, and internal knowledge bases, and the same content can be shared publicly or restricted to teams.

Developer-friendly features set it apart. Content can sync with a GitHub or GitLab repository, so docs can live alongside code and be reviewed through pull requests, and a change request workflow lets teams review edits before publishing. OpenAPI imports generate API reference pages, and integrations connect analytics, support tools, and chat. AI features include an assistant that answers readers’ questions from the docs, AI-enhanced search, and help with writing and editing pages.

item.title: Hive Moderation
item.description:
Hive offers content moderation as an API. A platform sends user uploads, such as photos, videos, livestreams, comments, or audio, and Hive returns classifications with confidence scores across categories like nudity, violence, hate symbols, drugs, and self-harm. Companies use these results to automatically remove content, send borderline cases to human reviewers, or restrict access, which would be impossible to do manually at scale.

The company’s models have broadened beyond traditional moderation. Hive offers AI-generated content detection to identify synthetic images, video, and audio, deepfake detection used by government and media customers, and tools for brand safety and contextual advertising. It trains on large human-labeled datasets, and customers can customize settings for their own policies.

item.title: Insomnia
item.description:
Insomnia is a desktop application that lets developers send requests to APIs and inspect responses. You build requests with headers, authentication, and bodies, organize them into collections, and use environment variables to switch between development and production. It supports REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket, and Server-Sent Events, and can import definitions from OpenAPI specifications.

Beyond manual testing, it supports design and automation. An API design editor helps write specs, test suites run collections of requests with assertions, and command-line tools run tests in CI. Plugins extend functionality, Git sync stores collections with code, and AI features help generate requests, tests, and documentation. Insomnia can store data locally or in the cloud, a choice that matters to teams concerned about privacy.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: Moralis
item.description:
Moralis provides ready-made APIs for blockchain data. Instead of reading raw blocks, developers can ask for a wallet’s token balances, NFT holdings, transaction history, or prices and receive clean results across multiple chains, such as Ethereum, Polygon, Solana, and others. This cuts down the time to build wallets, portfolio trackers, NFT marketplaces, and analytics tools.

Other products support app development. Authentication lets users sign in with their wallets, Streams delivers real-time notifications about on-chain events, and node access and data APIs support decentralized finance and gaming projects. Documentation and SDKs help developers integrate quickly, and the platform handles indexing and scaling.

item.title: Perspective API
item.description:
Perspective used machine learning to help moderate online conversations. A site sent a comment to the API and received scores for attributes such as toxicity, insult, profanity, and threat, which publishers and platforms used to flag comments for review, warn commenters before posting, or sort discussions. News organizations and forums used it to cope with large numbers of comments, and researchers used it to study online abuse.

The tool also sparked debate. Studies found that its scores could be biased, for example by rating comments mentioning certain identity terms as more toxic, and it was not a substitute for human moderators. Jigsaw acknowledged limitations and worked to reduce bias, and the model was widely used in research as a benchmark for toxicity.

item.title: Postman
item.description: Postman started as a simple way to send HTTP requests without writing code, and it is still the most common tool for poking at an API. You enter a URL, choose a method, add headers and a body, and see the response. Requests are saved in collections that can be shared with a team, and environments let you switch variables like base URLs and keys between development, staging, and production without editing every request.

item.title: RapidAPI
item.description:
RapidAPI made discovering APIs easier. Developers browse a catalog of thousands of APIs across categories such as weather, finance, sports, language, and AI, test them in the browser, and subscribe with a single key and billing account. This saves the effort of signing up with every provider separately, and API publishers get a distribution channel and billing.

The company also offered products for businesses, including an enterprise hub for managing internal and partner APIs, and testing tools. Nokia acquired the technology and marketplace to support its efforts to expose telecom network capabilities to developers through APIs, and the public marketplace is expected to continue much as before with some rebranding.

item.title: Repustate
item.description: Repustate focuses on understanding opinions in many languages. Its API reads text, such as tweets, reviews, news, or survey responses, and returns the sentiment, the topics and entities discussed, and the themes that recur, with attention to context so that sentiment about one aspect of a product can be separated from another. Language coverage is a selling point, including Arabic, Chinese, and many other languages that are less well served by some competitors.

item.title: Stripe
item.description: Stripe began as a way for developers to accept card payments with a few lines of code and has become the payment layer for much of the internet. Businesses use it to take cards and local payment methods online and in person, bill customers on subscription plans, send invoices, and pay out sellers on marketplaces. Its documentation and libraries are widely admired, which is why startups tend to adopt it first. It operates in many countries and currencies.

item.title: Agno
item.description:
Agno, formerly called Phidata, aims to make agent building straightforward and fast. A developer defines an agent in a few lines: choose a model, give it instructions and tools, and optionally attach memory and a knowledge base. Agents can search the web, query databases, call APIs, and work with text, images, and audio. Multiple agents can be combined into teams that collaborate on complex tasks.

The framework emphasizes performance and production use. It is designed to start agents quickly and use little memory, which helps when many run at once, and it includes features such as session storage, retrieval from vector databases, structured outputs, and reasoning steps. AgentOS, a runtime layer, lets teams serve agents through an API with a control interface, and monitoring tools show runs and performance.

item.title: AI For Developer
item.description:
AI For Developer is a niche directory focused on the developer audience. Instead of listing every AI product, it gathers tools that matter to people who write software: coding assistants, AI-powered editors, model APIs, testing and documentation tools, and infrastructure for building AI features. Listings give a short description, links, and categories, which makes it easy to browse by use case.

Directories like this serve as a starting point for discovery. They help developers learn what exists, compare similar tools, and keep up with the rapid pace of new launches. A curated approach aims to reduce the noise of general AI directories that include thousands of products across every field, by focusing on relevance to engineering.

item.title: AI21 Labs
item.description: AI21 Labs was founded by AI researchers in Tel Aviv and has been building language models since before ChatGPT made them mainstream. Its best-known models are the Jamba family, which blend a state-space architecture called Mamba with transformer layers. The aim is a model that handles very long documents with less memory and faster output than a standard transformer of similar size. Several Jamba versions have been released with open weights.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock
item.description: Bedrock is how many companies on AWS use large language models without running any model infrastructure. Instead of signing separate contracts with each AI lab, you pick from a catalog of models from providers such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and Amazon itself, and call them through one API. The data stays inside your AWS account, which matters to teams with security, privacy, and compliance requirements, and it works with the IAM, networking, and logging tools they already use.

item.title: Cartesia
item.description:
Cartesia focuses on speed in voice AI. Its Sonic models, built on state-space model architectures instead of only transformers, generate natural-sounding speech with very low latency, so a voice agent can start speaking almost as soon as a response is ready. That matters for phone calls and live assistants, where delays feel awkward. The company also offers voice cloning and control over emotion and speaking rate.

The platform has grown into a set of real-time voice building blocks. Sonic handles text-to-speech, Ink handles speech-to-text, and tools for managed voice agents help companies deploy agents that answer phone calls. Developers connect through APIs and SDKs, and Cartesia works with common voice agent frameworks and telephony providers. Multilingual support lets one system serve customers in different languages.

item.title: Cerebras
item.description:
Cerebras took an unusual approach to AI hardware. Instead of cutting a silicon wafer into many small chips, it builds a single enormous chip from the whole wafer, which holds an enormous amount of compute and on-chip memory. That design reduces the data movement between chips that slows down large models, and lets it generate tokens at very high speeds.

The company sells its systems and operates a cloud inference service where developers call open models through an API, with fast responses that suit agents, coding tools, and real-time applications. It has partnerships with AI labs and cloud providers, and supports training as well as inference. Developers can try the API with a free tier and then pay by usage, often at competitive per-token rates.

item.title: Chatbase
item.description: Chatbase started as a simple way to create a chatbot from your own data. You upload files, point it to a website, or connect sources such as Notion, and it builds an agent that answers questions using that information. You embed the chat widget on your site with a snippet of code and you have support available around the clock. The simplicity made it popular with small businesses and startups that wanted a support bot without engineering work.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Dify
item.description: Dify gives teams a visual way to build AI applications without writing everything from scratch. In its workflow editor, you connect blocks for models, prompts, knowledge retrieval, code, conditions, and tool calls to create chatbots, agents, and automations. Knowledge pipelines ingest documents, split and index them, and let the application answer questions from your own data. You can test and debug each run, then publish the app as a web interface or API.

item.title: Exa AI
item.description: Exa, formerly Metaphor, rethinks search for machines instead of people. Where a traditional engine matches keywords, Exa uses neural embeddings to find pages that are semantically similar to a query, even when they do not share words. You can search with natural-language descriptions, such as a list of startups building a specific kind of robot, and it returns results that match the idea. It can also take a link and find similar pages.

item.title: Fashwell
item.description:
Fashwell works on a persistent problem in online retail: product data is often incomplete or inconsistent. Its AI looks at product photos and automatically identifies attributes such as category, color, pattern, shape, neckline, and material, creating detailed, standardized tags. Those tags help retailers organize catalogs, improve search, and power filters that match how customers describe items.

The same technology supports discovery features. Visual search lets shoppers find similar items from an image, recommendation systems suggest products that match a style, and outfit and style-matching tools help shoppers complete a look. Retailers use it to save the effort of manual tagging across thousands of items and to improve the consistency of information across channels.

item.title: Fireworks AI
item.description:
Fireworks AI focuses on serving open models efficiently. Developers call popular open-weight language, vision, image, and speech models through an API compatible with OpenAI’s format, and the platform’s optimized inference engine delivers low latency and high throughput. Many companies use it to run models at a lower cost than closed alternatives and to maintain control over which models they use.

The platform goes beyond hosting. It supports fine-tuning on a company’s data, including reinforcement learning methods, deploys custom models, and handles structured outputs and function calling for building agents. Dedicated deployments offer reserved capacity for steady workloads, and features such as batch processing reduce cost for non-urgent jobs. It runs in the cloud, with enterprise options for security and compliance.

item.title: Foursquare
item.description:
Foursquare began as an app for checking in at places and discovering venues, but its main business today is location data. The company maintains a large database of points of interest, including businesses, landmarks, and venues, with details like categories, hours, and popularity. Developers use its Places API to add search, recommendations, and place information to maps and apps, and brands use its data to understand where people go.

Beyond place data, Foursquare provides tools for analyzing movement and location behavior. Panels of opted-in users allow measurement of foot traffic to stores, audience analysis, and attribution for advertising, and mapping and geospatial products let companies visualize and process location data at scale. Machine learning keeps place information up to date and helps match records from different sources.

item.title: Google AI Studio
item.description: Google AI Studio is where developers go to try Google’s models without setting anything up. You sign in with a Google account, pick a Gemini model, and start prompting in a playground that lets you adjust settings like temperature, add system instructions, and attach images, audio, video, or documents. Once a prompt works, one click gives you the code to run it through the Gemini API in Python, JavaScript, and other languages.

item.title: Google Translate
item.description: Google Translate is the translation tool most people try first. You type or paste text and get a translation in a second, with the language detected automatically. The mobile app adds the features travelers rely on: a camera mode that replaces text on signs and menus, a conversation mode that translates both sides of a spoken exchange, handwriting input, and offline language packs that work without a connection. Chrome can translate whole web pages, and you can upload documents and get a translated copy.

item.title: Groq
item.description: Groq is known for speed. Its chips, called Language Processing Units, were designed from scratch for running AI models rather than adapted from graphics hardware, and they produce text far faster than typical GPU-based services. That makes a difference for chat that feels instant, voice assistants that cannot afford to wait, and agents that make many model calls in a row. The company is not a model lab; it hosts models made by others.

item.title: Hugging Face
item.description: Hugging Face is often described as the GitHub of machine learning. Researchers and companies upload models and datasets to its Hub, where anyone can browse them, read the documentation, and download them. If an open model is released, whether a language model, an image generator, or a speech system, it almost always appears there first. Each model page has a card describing what it does, how it was trained, and how to use it, along with community discussions.

item.title: Infermedica
item.description:
Infermedica builds medical decision support for patient-facing use. A person answers questions about symptoms in an adaptive interview, and the system estimates likely conditions and recommends a level of care, such as self-care, a doctor visit, or emergency services. Organizations embed this in their apps and websites.

The engine rests on a medical knowledge base maintained by physicians, combined with probabilistic reasoning and language models for understanding free text. Use cases include directing patients to the right service, preparing clinicians with an intake summary, and reducing unnecessary visits.

item.title: Jan
item.description:
Jan lets you use language models without sending data anywhere. After installing the app, you browse a model hub, download models such as Llama, Mistral, or Qwen in a size your hardware can handle, and chat with them offline. Everything runs on your machine, which is attractive to people concerned about privacy or working without internet access, and it avoids per-use fees.

It is more than a chat window. Jan can connect to remote services like OpenAI and Anthropic with your own API keys, so you can switch between local and cloud models in one interface. A local server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so other tools can use your models, and support for the Model Context Protocol lets assistants use tools. The project also develops its own small models tuned for tasks.

item.title: LM Studio
item.description:
LM Studio makes running models on your own computer approachable. You open the app, search a catalog of models from Hugging Face, download one that fits your hardware, and start chatting, with no command line needed. Everything runs locally, so conversations stay on your machine, you can work offline, and there are no per-token fees. It supports popular open models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and gpt-oss.

For developers, LM Studio can start a local server that mimics the OpenAI API, so existing tools and scripts can point at your own model. It supports multiple model formats, including GGUF and Apple’s MLX for efficient performance on Mac, lets you tune settings such as context length and GPU offloading, and works with the Model Context Protocol to connect tools. A command-line version and SDKs support automation.

item.title: Microsoft Translator
item.description:
Microsoft Translator covers the common translation needs. You can type or paste text, speak into a phone for conversation translation, translate images and documents, and use offline language packs when traveling. Multi-device conversation mode lets several people speak in different languages and see translations on their own screens, which suits meetings and travel.

It’s integrated throughout Microsoft products. Teams offers live captions and translated meetings, Office apps can translate documents and text, and Edge translates web pages. For developers and businesses, Azure AI Translator provides APIs for text, document, and speech translation, with custom models and glossaries, and options to run in containers.

item.title: Mintlify
item.description:
Mintlify helps developer companies publish documentation that looks and works well. Teams write pages in MDX or Markdown, keep them in a Git repository, and Mintlify builds a fast, branded site with navigation, search, code samples, and API playgrounds generated from OpenAPI specs. Many well-known developer tools use it.

AI is part of both the reader and writer experience. An assistant on the docs site answers questions from the documentation, helping users find what they need, and docs are published in forms that AI coding tools can read, such as llms.txt and MCP servers. For writers, AI agents can draft pages, update docs when code changes, and flag outdated content. Analytics show what readers search for and where they get stuck.

item.title: Moovly
item.description:
Moovly serves companies that need many versions of the same video. Using a template, teams can generate hundreds or thousands of variations that change names, products, languages, or data, such as personalized sales videos or product videos for each item in a catalog. A browser editor handles design, and an API automates production from spreadsheets or other systems.

Localization is a major theme. Moovly can add subtitles, translate scripts, and generate voiceovers in multiple languages using AI voices, helping companies serve international audiences, and AI tools assist with text-to-video and editing. It’s used in marketing, e-commerce, training, and communications, and offers brand controls and collaboration for large teams.

item.title: Numerous
item.description:
Numerous brings language models into the spreadsheet. After installing the add-in, you use a formula such as =AI(“prompt”, cell) in a cell to ask the model to do something with the data: categorize customer feedback, write product descriptions, extract names from messy text, translate, or summarize. Filling the formula down a column performs the task on hundreds or thousands of rows, which would take hours by hand.

It aims to be approachable for people who know spreadsheets but not code. Prompts are written in plain language, results appear in cells where you can filter and calculate with them, and features help with common tasks like cleaning, tagging, and brainstorming. Marketers, e-commerce teams, researchers, and operations staff use it to process lists of items quickly.

item.title: Ollama
item.description:
Ollama made local AI simple. You install it, run a command such as ollama run with a model name, and it downloads the model and starts a chat in your terminal. It handles the details of quantization and GPU acceleration, so models like Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, and many others run on ordinary laptops and desktops. Everything stays on your machine, so it’s private and works offline.

It is a building block for developers. Ollama exposes a local REST API, including an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so apps and tools can use your local models, and many projects such as Open WebUI, coding assistants, and agent frameworks integrate with it. Modelfiles let you customize system prompts and parameters, and recent versions add a desktop app, support for multimodal models, and optional cloud-hosted models for those too big to run locally.

item.title: OpenAI Operator
item.description: Operator was OpenAI’s first widely available computer-using agent. It ran a browser in the cloud and looked at screenshots of web pages, then clicked, typed, and scrolled like a person to carry out a task such as ordering groceries, filling out a form, or booking a restaurant. You could watch it work, take control, and it paused to ask for confirmation before steps such as payments or entering sensitive details.

item.title: OpenAI Realtime API
item.description:
The Realtime API changes how voice applications are built. Older systems chained speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis, adding delay at each step. The Realtime API handles audio in and audio out directly in one model, so responses start sooner and can include tone, pauses, and interruptions that sound natural.

Developers connect over WebRTC or WebSockets to stream audio and receive speech, text, and tool calls. It supports function calling, so a voice agent can look up data or take actions, and it can be used for phone agents, in-app assistants, and language practice.

item.title: OpenRouter
item.description:
OpenRouter solves the problem of juggling many AI provider accounts. A developer gets one API key and one endpoint, and can call any supported model by changing its name, using the same request format as OpenAI’s API. Billing is unified, with credits that work across providers, which makes it easy to try new models as soon as they appear, including open-source ones hosted by different companies.

Beyond routing, it adds useful features. Automatic fallbacks switch to another provider if one is down, routing options choose the cheapest or fastest provider for a model, and analytics show usage and cost. Public rankings show which models people use most, giving a view of real-world adoption. Users can bring their own provider keys and set data privacy preferences that control which providers may see their prompts.

item.title: Perplexity Sonar
item.description:
Sonar lets developers build apps that answer questions using current web information. Instead of relying only on a model’s training data, a request to Sonar searches the web, reads relevant pages, and returns a response with citations. That grounding is useful for assistants, research tools, news summaries, and any product where freshness and sources matter.

There are several variants. The standard Sonar models are fast and low-cost, Sonar Pro handles more complex queries with more sources, Sonar Reasoning adds step-by-step analysis, and Sonar Deep Research runs multi-step research jobs and writes longer reports. A Search API offers ranked web results for developers who want to feed content to their own models. The API follows a format familiar to users of OpenAI’s, so adoption is simple, and options control which domains to search and how recent results should be.

item.title: Replica Studios
item.description:
Replica Studios was an Australian startup that made AI voices aimed at creative productions. Its library offered voices of professional actors who had agreed to license their performances, and its tools let game developers and filmmakers generate dialogue with emotion and style. Integrations for game engines such as Unreal and Unity made it easy to put placeholder or final voices into a project, and it also supported voice conversion.

The company drew attention for working with actors instead of against them. It signed an agreement with the actors’ union SAG-AFTRA on terms for licensing digital voice replicas in games, which some actors welcomed and others criticized as inadequate. That debate was part of a wider fight over how AI voices should be used in entertainment, which continues.

item.title: Resemble AI
item.description: Resemble AI builds voices for products and productions. You provide recordings of a speaker, with consent, and the platform trains a voice model that can read any text in that voice, or convert one person’s speech into another voice in real time. Companies use it for branded voices, localization, games, call centers, and media. An API makes it possible to generate speech in applications, and the system supports multiple languages and emotional control.

item.title: Stability AI
item.description:
Stability AI helped start the open-source image generation boom with Stable Diffusion, a model anyone could download, run, and modify. The release spurred a huge community of tools, fine-tunes, and applications, and changed expectations about access to generative models.

The company has since released a family of models, including newer image generators, Stable Video Diffusion, Stable Audio for music and sound, and 3D tools. It sells API access and commercial licenses, and partners with enterprises, and with media and entertainment companies.

item.title: Together AI
item.description:
Together AI focuses on open models. Developers call popular open-weight models for text, code, images, and more through an OpenAI-compatible API, and the platform’s optimized inference stack delivers speed and competitive prices. It includes serverless endpoints for quick use, dedicated endpoints for steady workloads, and batch processing to reduce cost.

The company also supports customization and training. Teams can fine-tune models on their data, including with reinforcement methods, and rent GPU clusters for large training runs, with an emphasis on cutting-edge hardware. Together’s researchers have contributed techniques such as FlashAttention that improve model efficiency, which feeds into its products.

item.title: Together AI
item.description:
Together AI hosts open models such as Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek, and offers a developer-friendly API compatible with common formats. Its inference stack is tuned for speed, and options range from pay-per-token serverless access to dedicated endpoints for steady workloads.

Customization is a second focus. Teams can fine-tune models on their data, train at scale on GPU clusters, and run batch jobs at lower cost. The company’s research contributions in efficient attention and inference feed into its products.

item.title: Weather.ai
item.description:
Weather.ai positions itself as a forecast service built on machine learning rather than only traditional physics models. It aims to give hourly and daily forecasts for specific locations, which is the kind of hyperlocal output people want for planning a run, a trip, or an event. The site focuses on readable forecasts, and an API is available for developers.

Machine learning is now common in weather prediction. Large research efforts from Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and others have shown that models trained on decades of observations can produce competitive forecasts quickly, and many startups sell tailored predictions built on this work. Services in this space usually combine public data from national weather agencies with their own models and corrections.

item.title: Codemod
item.description:
Codemod targets a chore every large codebase faces: changing the same pattern in hundreds or thousands of places. Codemods are scripts that rewrite code programmatically, for example moving from one version of a framework to the next. The platform provides a registry of community codemods, tools to run them, and a way to write new ones.

AI makes creating codemods easier. A developer describes a migration, and the tool helps produce the transformation and test it on examples, then applies it across repositories and opens pull requests for review. This turns weeks of manual edits into a reviewable change.

item.title: Fal.ai
item.description:
fal.ai gives developers a fast way to use generative media models without managing GPUs. A team calls an API for models that produce images, video, audio, and 3D assets, and fal handles the infrastructure, scaling, and optimization. Its speed is the main pitch, which matters for apps where users wait on each generation.

The catalog includes popular open models and models from partners, and the platform is used by consumer apps, design tools, and companies that add generation features to their products. Developers can also deploy their own models and fine-tunes on its serverless compute, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Fish Audio
item.description:
Fish Audio generates synthetic speech with an emphasis on voice variety. Users type text, choose a voice, and get audio. A cloning feature creates a voice from a short sample, and a public library offers voices shared by other users, including character and celebrity-style options.

Creators use it for narration, videos, games, and podcasts, and developers integrate it through an API for apps and agents. The company has released open models for speech synthesis, which has helped it build a community of users and researchers.

item.title: Gladia
item.description:
Gladia provides speech-to-text as a service for developers. Companies send audio from calls, meetings, or videos and receive transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and optional translation. It handles dozens of languages and can detect which one is being spoken.

Real-time transcription suits live captioning and voice agents, while batch processing handles recordings at scale. Extra features include summaries, sentiment, and named entity detection. The API is aimed at products built on audio, such as meeting assistants, call analytics, and media tools.

item.title: Helicone
item.description:
Helicone gives teams visibility into their language model usage. A developer changes the base URL of their API calls to route through Helicone, and each request is logged with its prompt, response, latency, cost, and user. Dashboards show spend by model, user, or feature, and flag errors.

Additional tools help manage production use. Caching saves cost on repeated requests, rate limits protect budgets, and prompt management lets teams version and test prompts. Sessions group multi-step agent traces, and evaluation features score outputs.

item.title: Jina AI
item.description:
Jina AI focuses on the retrieval side of AI applications. Its embedding models turn text and images into vectors for search in many languages, rerankers sort results by relevance, and a reader API converts a web page into clean text that language models can use. Search and deep research endpoints build on these.

Many developers used Jina’s open models from Hugging Face and its free-to-start APIs when building retrieval-augmented generation. The company also open-sourced framework projects for building multimodal systems in its early years.

item.title: Lakera
item.description:
Lakera defends applications built on language models. Its Guard product sits between users and a model, scanning prompts for attempts to override instructions, extract secrets, or inject malicious content, and checking outputs for leaks and harmful material. Developers add it with an API call.

The company grew out of research on adversarial attacks and became known for Gandalf, a public game where players try to trick a model into revealing a password, which generated a large dataset of attacks. Red teaming tools test applications before launch.

item.title: MultiOn
item.description:
MultiOn was one of the early companies to build browser-using agents. A user gives an instruction in plain language, and the agent navigates sites, clicks, types, and completes the steps, keeping a session going across pages. Developers could call it through an API to build agents of their own.

The company has talked about moving into a new phase, and directories describe a change of name and focus, though accounts differ. That makes it worth checking the official site to see what is currently available before depending on it.

item.title: Portkey
item.description:
Portkey sits between applications and model providers. Developers send requests to Portkey, which forwards them to the chosen provider and handles retries, fallbacks to other models, caching, and load balancing. This increases reliability and makes it easy to switch models.

The platform adds visibility and governance: logs and analytics on cost and latency, prompt management, guardrails that check inputs and outputs, and budgets and access controls for teams. It supports the Model Context Protocol and agent frameworks.

item.title: Prefect
item.description:
Prefect lets developers turn Python functions into reliable workflows. By adding decorators, a script becomes a flow with tasks that retry on failure, run on a schedule, and report state. Teams view runs, logs, and results in a dashboard.

It supports dynamic workflows, concurrency, and deployment to different infrastructure, from a laptop to Kubernetes. A hosted cloud service handles scheduling and observability, and the open-source server can be self-hosted. It is used for data pipelines and machine learning jobs.

item.title: PromptLayer
item.description:
PromptLayer separates prompts from code. Teams store prompts in a registry, version them, test changes against datasets, and deploy new versions without redeploying the application. Non-engineers, such as product managers and domain experts, can edit prompts in a visual interface.

Observability features log every call with inputs, outputs, cost, and latency, and let teams search and analyze history. Evaluations compare prompt versions and models, and workflows chain steps for agents.

item.title: Reducto
item.description:
Reducto turns messy documents into clean data. A developer sends a PDF or image, and the API returns structured output that preserves layout, tables, and figures, which can feed language models or databases. It combines vision models and traditional techniques to handle difficult pages.

Applications include financial analysis, legal review, healthcare records, and RAG systems where poor parsing hurts answer quality. Options exist for extracting fields to a schema and for splitting documents by type. Enterprises can deploy it in their own environment.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Tavily
item.description:
Tavily provides web search for machines. A developer sends a query and receives ranked results with cleaned content and sources, trimmed to what a language model needs, so agents can ground answers in current information. Extra endpoints extract text from pages, crawl sites, and run deeper research.

It integrates with frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex and with the Model Context Protocol, which made it a common choice for adding web access to agents. A free tier supports experimentation.

item.title: Amazon Polly
item.description:
Polly takes text and returns audio, which developers call from their apps to add speech. It offers dozens of voices across many languages and accents, built on several engines. The neural voices sound considerably more natural than the older standard ones, and newer generative voices push realism further. It is used for reading articles aloud, voicing phone systems and assistants, creating e-learning narration, and adding accessibility features to apps.

Control over how things are said is a strength. SSML tags let you adjust pauses, emphasis, pitch, speed, and the way numbers, dates, and abbreviations are spoken. Custom lexicons teach Polly the right pronunciation of brand names and jargon. It can also return speech marks that tell your app when each word is spoken, which is useful for highlighting text in sync with audio. Output can be streamed or saved as files in common formats.

item.title: AssemblyAI
item.description:
AssemblyAI is infrastructure for apps that need to understand speech. A developer sends audio from a call, meeting, podcast, or video, and the API returns an accurate transcript with word-level timestamps. It supports pre-recorded files and real-time streaming, so it can power live captions and voice assistants as well as batch transcription. Customers use it to build call analytics, meeting note takers, media search, and compliance tools.

Beyond transcription, a layer of speech understanding turns text into structured data. It can separate speakers, summarize a conversation, detect topics, and score sentiment. Guardrails features redact personal information and filter sensitive content before the data goes anywhere else. An LLM Gateway lets developers pass transcripts to language models for tasks like extracting action items, and a voice agent API supports speech-to-speech applications.

item.title: Deepgram
item.description:
Deepgram sells speech AI to developers. Its speech-to-text API transcribes audio in real time or from recordings, and it is designed for accuracy at low latency and low cost, which matters for call centers, meeting tools, and voice assistants that process large volumes. Features include speaker labeling, punctuation, keyword boosting, and support for many languages, and models can be customized to a company’s vocabulary.

The platform has widened to cover the whole voice stack. A text-to-speech product generates natural voices with low latency, and a voice agent API combines speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis into a single service for building conversational agents that can hold phone calls. Enterprises can run Deepgram in their own cloud or on-premises when data cannot leave their control.

item.title: Kokoro TTS
item.description:
Kokoro is notable for doing a lot with a little. The model is small enough to run on a laptop, a phone, or a modest server, yet produces speech that many listeners find clear and natural in several voices. That makes it practical for local and low-cost deployments.

Developers use it for narration, accessibility tools, voice agents, and offline applications, and community projects have packaged it for the browser and for popular frameworks. The license is permissive, which allows commercial use, and the weights are available on Hugging Face.

item.title: Meshy
item.description:
Meshy makes 3D asset creation fast. You type a description or upload an image, and it generates a 3D mesh with textures in a minute or two. The results can be rotated, refined, and downloaded in common formats. Indie game developers, 3D printing hobbyists, product designers, and virtual world builders use it to produce props, characters, and environment pieces without modeling each from scratch.

The platform includes tools for the steps after generation. It can retexture a model from a prompt, remesh to adjust polygon counts and topology, and add skeletons and animations to characters. Plugins and an API connect it with Blender, Unity, Unreal Engine, Maya, and other tools, so assets can flow into existing pipelines. A library of community models provides starting points.

item.title: Mubert
item.description:
Mubert generates music in real time. You pick a mood, genre, or activity, such as focus, workout, or sleep, and it streams a continuous track that does not loop in an obvious way. Creators use it for background music in videos, streams, podcasts, and apps, and the royalty-free licensing makes it practical for online content.

Several products serve different needs. Mubert Render lets users create tracks of a chosen length from a text prompt or style, and a mobile app offers streaming for listening. An API allows developers to add generated music to games, fitness apps, and other products, delivering music that adapts to context. Artists can contribute sounds to the system, with revenue sharing for contributors.

item.title: MySpec
item.description:
MySpec starts with the plan instead of the code. A user describes a product or feature, and the platform produces a specification covering requirements, architecture, and tasks. That document guides the build, whether a human or an AI coding agent does the work.

The idea responds to a common problem: coding agents given vague prompts produce inconsistent results. A clear spec gives the agent a target and gives the team something to review before time is spent. It fits the approach seen in tools like Kiro and GitHub’s Spec Kit.

item.title: Photoroom
item.description:
Photoroom grew from a background remover into a full product photography tool. Take a picture of a product on a table, and the app cuts it out cleanly, then places it on a white background, a color, or an AI-generated scene with realistic shadows and lighting. For small sellers on marketplaces like Etsy, eBay, and Shopify, that means professional-looking listings without a studio.

Other features expand the range. An AI backgrounds tool creates settings from a text description, an instant shadow and relight tool adds depth, and a magic retouch removes objects and blemishes. Templates in standard sizes speed up posts for social media and marketplaces. Batch editing handles whole catalogs, and an API lets platforms add the same processing to their own apps. Teams can share brand templates.

item.title: PlayHT
item.description: PlayHT offered realistic text-to-speech with a large catalog of voices across many languages, plus voice cloning from short audio samples. Creators used its web studio to narrate videos, podcasts, and audiobooks, and developers used its API to add speech to apps and phone systems. Its later conversational models were built to sound natural in dialogue, with emotion and pacing, and the company also developed voice agents under the PlayAI name.

item.title: Remove.bg
item.description:
Remove.bg made background removal fast and easy. You upload a photo, or drag it onto the page, and an AI model detects the foreground and returns the image with a transparent background in a few seconds. It handles people, products, animals, and cars, and it copes reasonably well with difficult edges like hair and fur. It is used for e-commerce product photos, profile pictures, ID photos, and design mockups.

The service extends beyond the website. Plugins connect it to Photoshop, Figma, and other tools, apps let you process images on a phone or desktop, and an API allows platforms to add automatic background removal at scale. Once the background is removed, you can add a solid color, a template, or another image. Bulk tools handle large catalogs. Remove.bg is owned by Canva.

item.title: Replicate
item.description: Replicate makes it easy to use machine learning models without managing servers. A developer picks a model from a large public library, such as an image generator, a speech tool, a video model, or a language model, and calls it through a few lines of code. The platform handles GPUs, scaling, and versioning, and charges by the second of compute, so costs track real use. Many hobbyist and startup apps rely on it.
